subject: Medicine
topic: Inpatient Glycemic Targets Scheduled Basal-Bolus vs Sliding-Scale Insulin
stem: A 64-year-old man with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to the general medicine hospitalist service for intravenous antibiotic treatment of right lower extremity cellulitis. Prior to admission, his home diabetes regimen consisted of metformin 1,000 mg twice daily and glipizide 10 mg daily. On admission, his temperature is 38.4 C, blood pressure 134/78 mm Hg, and heart rate 92/min. Laboratory evaluation reveals: WBC count 14,200/uL, serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, and random blood glucose 246 mg/dL; baseline HbA1c obtained 2 weeks ago was 8.8%. He is tolerating a consistent carbohydrate diabetic diet. An admitting resident suggests placing the patient on a sliding-scale regular insulin protocol alone and holding all other diabetic medications. Which of the following represents the most appropriate, guideline-directed inpatient glycemic management strategy for this non-critically ill patient?

options.text: Discontinuation of oral agents and initiation of a scheduled basal-bolus-correction insulin regimen targeting blood glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL
options.explanation: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and Endocrine Society inpatient glycemic management guidelines, the standard of care for non-critically ill hospitalized patients with diabetes is: (1) DISCONTINUATION OF ORAL HYPOGLYCEMIC AGENTS: Metformin is withheld during hospitalization due to the risk of lactic acidosis if renal function fluctuates or iodinated contrast is administered; sulfonylureas (glipizide) are held due to unpredictable oral intake and prolonged hypoglycemia risks; (2) INITIATION OF SCHEDULED BASAL-BOLUS-CORRECTION INSULIN: For patients with adequate nutritional intake, a physiologic three-component insulin regimen is mandatory: (a) Basal insulin (long-acting glargine or degludec, providing ~50% of total daily dose) to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis; (b) Nutritional/prandial bolus insulin (rapid-acting lispro, aspart, or glulisine, ~50% of total daily dose divided before meals); and (c) Supplemental/correction insulin for pre-meal hyperglycemia; (3) INPATIENT GLYCEMIC TARGET: A target blood glucose range of 140 TO 180 MG/DL (7.8 to 10.0 mmol/L) is recommended for the vast majority of non-critically ill hospitalized patients. Tighter targets (<110-140 mg/dL) do not improve clinical outcomes and dramatically increase dangerous hypoglycemia; and (4) SLIDING-SCALE INSULIN ALONE IS STRONGLY DISCOURAGED: Sliding-scale regular insulin monotherapy is purely reactive (treating hyperglycemia only after it occurs) and is associated with severe glycemic variability, prolonged hospitalization, and higher rates of hospital-acquired infections (RABBIT-2 trial).

options.text: Continuation of home oral metformin and glipizide with strict fasting blood glucose targets of 80 to 110 mg/dL
options.explanation: Oral agents are unsafe during acute illness due to acute kidney injury and hypoglycemia; tight targets (<110 mg/dL) increase fatal hypoglycemia without benefit.

options.text: Implementation of a sliding-scale regular insulin monotherapy protocol without any scheduled basal insulin
options.explanation: Sliding-scale monotherapy treats hyperglycemia reactively and was definitively shown in the RABBIT-2 trial to increase glycemic variability and complications.

options.text: Continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion targeting blood glucose 100 to 130 mg/dL on the general ward
options.explanation: Continuous intravenous insulin infusions are reserved for the intensive care unit and diabetic ketoacidosis, not stable cellulitis on a general medical floor.

options.text: Withholding all insulin therapy unless random blood glucose exceeds 300 mg/dL to avoid hypoglycemia
options.explanation: Permissive severe hyperglycemia (>200-300 mg/dL) impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and wound healing, escalating cellulitis progression.

subject: Medicine
topic: Perioperative Anticoagulation Bridging Management in Atrial Fibrillation
stem: A 72-year-old man with permanent nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and hypertension is scheduled to undergo an elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy for a benign colonic adenoma in 6 days. Current medications include warfarin 5 mg daily and lisinopril 20 mg daily. His international normalized ratio (INR) today is 2.4. He has no history of stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or systemic thromboembolism. His calculated CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (age 72, hypertension). The surgical team requests guidance regarding perioperative anticoagulation management. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan regarding perioperative bridging anticoagulation for this patient?

options.text: Discontinuation of warfarin 5 days prior to surgery with initiation of therapeutic subcutaneous enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily bridging
options.explanation: Routine LMWH bridging in moderate-risk atrial fibrillation was proven in the BRIDGE trial to triple major bleeding without reducing perioperative stroke.

options.text: Discontinuation of warfarin 5 days prior to surgery without any low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) bridging therapy
options.explanation: This patient has NONVALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION with a MODERATE ISCHEMIC STROKE RISK (CHA2DS2-VASc = 3, corresponding to an annualized stroke risk of ~3-4%, or an absolute 8-day perioperative stroke risk of <0.1%). The landmark BRIDGE (Bridging Anticoagulation in Patients who Require Temporary Interruption of Warfarin Therapy) randomized trial and contemporary CHEST / ACC guidelines established that: (1) ROUTINE PERIOPERATIVE BRIDGING ANTICOAGULATION WITH THERAPEUTIC LMWH (enoxaparin) DOES NOT REDUCE ARTERIAL THROMBOEMBOLISM IN PATIENTS WITH NONVALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION; and (2) BRIDGING SIGNIFICANTLY INCREASES THE RISK OF MAJOR BLEEDING BY MORE THAN THREE-FOLD (3.2% vs 1.3%). Therefore, for patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with low-to-moderate stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc <= 4 without prior stroke), WARFARIN SHOULD BE DISCONTINUED 5 DAYS PRIOR TO SURGERY (allowing INR to normalize to <= 1.4) WITHOUT ANY LMWH BRIDGING. Bridging anticoagulation is reserved strictly for HIGH THROMBOEMBOLIC RISK scenarios: (a) Any mechanical mitral valve prosthesis; (b) Older-generation mechanical aortic valve (caged-ball/tilting disc); (c) Recent ischemic stroke or TIA within the past 3 months; or (d) Recent venous thromboembolism within the past 3 months.

options.text: Continuation of full-dose warfarin uninterrupted throughout the laparoscopic colon resection
options.explanation: Continuing therapeutic warfarin through major intra-abdominal surgery causes catastrophic operative hemorrhage and hematoma formation.

options.text: Administration of intravenous vitamin K 10 mg the evening prior to surgery to accelerate INR normalization
options.explanation: Routine vitamin K for elective surgical reversal causes refractory warfarin resistance for days postoperatively; stopping warfarin 5 days prior is sufficient.

options.text: Discontinuation of warfarin 10 days prior to surgery with initiation of oral aspirin 325 mg daily as bridging
options.explanation: Aspirin bridging does not prevent cardioembolic stroke and impairs surgical platelet hemostasis, increasing operative blood loss.

subject: Geriatrics
topic: Hospital Delirium Multicomponent Non-Pharmacological Prevention Bundle
stem: An 81-year-old woman is admitted to the hospitalist service for community-acquired pneumonia. She has a history of mild vascular dementia (baseline functional dependence with meal preparation) and hypertension. She is treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin, supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/min, and an indwelling Foley catheter placed in the emergency department. On hospital night 2, the night nurse calls the cross-covering resident reporting that the patient has become acutely agitated, is pulling at her intravenous line, believes she is trapped in a bus station, and is disoriented to time and place. Vital signs: blood pressure 138/80 mm Hg, heart rate 84/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96%. Physical examination reveals an agitated woman with fluctuating attention; cardiopulmonary examination is unchanged, and there are no focal neurological deficits. Blood glucose is 128 mg/dL, and electrolyte panel is normal. The nurse asks for an order for intravenous haloperidol or lorazepam to calm the patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Administration of intravenous haloperidol 2 mg every 4 hours scheduled around the clock for 48 hours
options.explanation: Routine scheduled antipsychotics do not resolve delirium or improve survival, and significantly increase mortality, ventricular arrhythmias, and extrapyramidal toxicity.

options.text: Administration of intravenous lorazepam 1 mg every 2 hours as needed for agitation
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in older adults, cause paradoxical disinhibition, double fall risk, and are contraindicated outside alcohol/sedative withdrawal.

options.text: Implementation of a multicomponent non-pharmacological delirium bundle (removal of the Foley catheter, reorientation, mobilization, sleep hygiene) and withholding routine antipsychotics
options.explanation: This patient has ACUTE HOSPITAL DELIRIUM (hyperactive/mixed subtype), characterized by an acute onset and fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition, triggered by systemic infection, unfamiliar hospital surroundings, and tethering devices (Foley catheter, IV lines). The American Geriatrics Society (AGS) and Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) guidelines establish: (1) NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL MULTICOMPONENT INTERVENTIONS (Hospital Elder Life Program [HELP] model) ARE THE FIRST-LINE AND ONLY INTERVENTIONS PROVEN TO REDUCE DELIRIUM DURATION AND SEVERITY. Core interventions include: (a) Early removal of physical restraints and tethering medical devices (IMMEDIATE REMOVAL OF INDWELLING FOLEY CATHETERS, which cause substantial delirium, agitation, and CAUTIs); (b) Frequent reorientation by familiar staff and family members; (c) Cognitive stimulation; (d) Early physical mobilization; (e) Sensory aids (ensuring eyeglasses and hearing aids are in place); and (f) Environmental sleep hygiene (minimizing nighttime vitals, lighting, and noise); (2) PHARMACOTHERAPY SHOULD BE WITHHELD FOR ROUTINE DELIRIUM: Antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine) DO NOT REDUCE DELIRIUM DURATION, RESOLUTION, ICU STAY, OR MORTALITY, and carry severe risks of QTc prolongation, extrapyramidal symptoms, and stroke; and (3) BENZODIAZEPINES (lorazepam) EXACERBATE DELIRIUM and are strictly contraindicated unless delirium is caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal.

options.text: Application of bilateral soft wrist restraints to secure the peripheral intravenous catheter
options.explanation: Physical restraints worsen delirium severity, increase psychological trauma, cause injury from struggling, and do not prevent line dislodgement.

options.text: Immediate unenhanced head CT scanning followed by emergent lumbar puncture
options.explanation: In a hospitalized patient with known pneumonia and fluctuating attention without focal neurologic deficits, routine neuroimaging and LP are low-yield.

subject: Medicine
topic: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome Symptom-Triggered vs Fixed-Schedule Benzodiazepines
stem: A 48-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol consumption (consuming approximately a fifth of vodka daily for 10 years) is admitted to the hospitalist service with an acute non-displaced right bimalleolar ankle fracture sustained in a fall. He underwent closed reduction and splinting in the emergency department. Approximately 16 hours after his last alcoholic drink, he develops fine resting tremors of both outstretched hands, profuse diaphoresis, nausea, anxiety, and a heart rate of 114/min with blood pressure 156/94 mm Hg. He is fully oriented to person, place, and time. He has no prior history of delirium tremens or alcohol withdrawal seizures. Physical examination reveals an anxious, tremulous man without focal neurological deficits. An admitting intern proposes placing the patient on a fixed-schedule regimen of oral chlordiazepoxide 50 mg every 6 hours around the clock for 4 days. Which of the following represents the most appropriate, evidence-based management strategy for this patient's alcohol withdrawal?

options.text: Institution of a fixed-schedule chlordiazepoxide regimen with additional as-needed boluses for 7 days
options.explanation: Fixed-schedule regimens administer large cumulative doses of long-acting sedatives regardless of actual need, causing excessive sedation and prolonged hospital stay.

options.text: Prescribing oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily as non-benzodiazepine monotherapy for withdrawal
options.explanation: Baclofen is an adjunctive agent for craving reduction; it has zero proven efficacy in preventing life-threatening withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.

options.text: Administration of intravenous phenytoin loading dose 1,000 mg to prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures
options.explanation: Phenytoin and antiepileptic drugs are completely ineffective for preventing or treating alcohol withdrawal seizures; GABA-ergic benzodiazepines are required.

options.text: Implementation of a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocol using the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) scale
options.explanation: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME (AWS) results from the abrupt cessation of alcohol in chronic drinkers, leading to central nervous system hyperarousal due to decreased GABA-A receptor inhibitory activity and uninhibited NMDA glutamate receptor excitation. The American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) guidelines strongly establish that: (1) SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED BENZODIAZEPINE THERAPY IS SUPERIOR TO FIXED-SCHEDULE REGIMENS. In a symptom-triggered protocol, a validated clinical tool (such as the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised [CIWA-Ar]) is scored by nursing every 1 to 2 hours. Benzodiazepines (e.g., oral lorazepam 2 mg, chlordiazepoxide 50 mg, or diazepam 10-20 mg) are administered ONLY WHEN THE CIWA-Ar SCORE EXCEEDS A SPECIFIED THRESHOLD (typically >= 8 to 10 for mild-moderate withdrawal); (2) ADVANTAGES: Randomized trials (Saitz et al.) demonstrated that symptom-triggered therapy REDUCES TOTAL BENZODIAZEPINE DOSAGE BY OVER 75% (preventing iatrogenic over-sedation and respiratory depression) and SIGNIFICANTLY SHORTENS THE DURATION OF DETOXIFICATION (from 68 hours down to 9 hours) while providing identical protection against seizures and delirium tremens; and (3) Fixed-schedule regimens are reserved only for patients who cannot be reliably assessed (e.g., intubated patients or uncooperative individuals).

options.text: Administration of intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as monotherapy to suppress autonomic hyperarousal
options.explanation: Antipsychotics (haloperidol) lower the seizure threshold in alcohol withdrawal and are strictly contraindicated as monotherapy for withdrawal tremors.

subject: Medicine
topic: Tumor Lysis Syndrome Rasburicase Contraindication in G6PD Deficiency
stem: A 24-year-old man of African descent is admitted to the hematology-oncology service with newly diagnosed high-grade Burkitt lymphoma. He has massive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and an extremely high tumor proliferative fraction (Ki-67 >99%). Baseline laboratory testing prior to chemotherapy demonstrates: WBC 42,000/uL, serum uric acid 14.8 mg/dL (markedly elevated, reference <7.5 mg/dL), serum potassium 5.2 mEq/L, serum phosphorus 6.4 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). He is diagnosed with laboratory and clinical TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME (TLS). Aggressive intravenous hydration is initiated. The oncology team plans to administer intravenous rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) to rapidly lower his serum uric acid before starting induction chemotherapy. Which of the following is the most critical screening step or contraindication that must be evaluated prior to the administration of rasburicase?

options.text: Screening for HLA-B*5801 allele, as rasburicase carries an extreme risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
options.explanation: HLA-B*5801 screening is mandatory for ALLOPURINOL hypersensitivity syndrome (especially in Southeast Asian patients), not for rasburicase.

options.text: Baseline measurement of serum xanthine oxidase activity to determine appropriate rasburicase weight-based dosing
options.explanation: Rasburicase acts directly on uric acid, bypassing xanthine oxidase; xanthine oxidase assays have no role in rasburicase dosing.

options.text: Assessing for baseline hypercalcemia, as rasburicase administration triggers rapid calcium-phosphate precipitation
options.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome causes HYPOcalcemia (due to phosphate binding), not hypercalcemia, and rasburicase does not affect serum calcium.

options.text: Evaluation of baseline creatinine clearance, as rasburicase is renally cleared and contraindicated in renal failure
options.explanation: Rasburicase is cleared through peptide catabolism (independent of renal function) and is specifically indicated in renal insufficiency from uric acid nephropathy.

options.text: Screening for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, as rasburicase is absolutely contraindicated due to risk of fatal methemoglobinemia and severe hemolysis
options.explanation: RASBURICASE is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that catalyzes the enzymatic conversion of uric acid into ALLANTOIN, a highly water-soluble inactive metabolite that is 5 to 10 times more soluble than uric acid and easily cleared renally. Unlike allopurinol (which merely prevents new uric acid synthesis by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, leaving pre-existing uric acid intact), rasburicase actively degrades existing uric acid pools, reducing serum uric acid levels to near zero within 4 hours. However, rasburicase has an ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: GLUCOSE-6-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (G6PD) DEFICIENCY. The biochemical mechanism of rasburicase's enzymatic reaction generates HYDROGEN PEROXIDE (H2O2) as an equimolar byproduct. In individuals with normal G6PD activity, erythrocyte glutathione reductase detoxifies H2O2. In patients with G6PD deficiency, erythrocytes lack sufficient NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione; the unchecked hydrogen peroxide causes MASSIVE OXIDATIVE ERYTHROCYTE INJURY, PRECIPITATING SEVERE ACUTE HEMOLYTIC ANEMIA AND METHEMOGLOBINEMIA (cyanosis refractory to oxygen). FDA product labeling mandates that patients at high risk of G6PD deficiency (African, Mediterranean, or Southeast Asian ancestry) MUST BE SCREENED FOR G6PD DEFICIENCY PRIOR TO RASBURICASE; if G6PD deficiency is present, rasburicase is strictly contraindicated, and allopurinol plus aggressive hydration must be used.

subject: Medicine
topic: Contrast-Associated Acute Kidney Injury Intravenous Volume Expansion Prevention
stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, estimated GFR 36 mL/min/1.73 m2) is admitted for evaluation of suspected critical limb-threatening ischemia with a non-healing right great toe ulcer. A contrast-enhanced digital subtraction angiogram (DSA) of the right lower extremity is scheduled. He has no history of congestive heart failure, and physical examination reveals clear lung fields and no peripheral edema. Vital signs are normal. The vascular surgery fellow asks what prophylactic pharmacological regimen should be ordered to prevent CONTRAST-ASSOCIATED ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (CA-AKI). Which of the following is the most evidence-based, guideline-directed preventive strategy according to the PRESERVE trial and KDIGO guidelines?

options.text: Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (0.9% normal saline or Lactated Ringer's) administered pre- and post-procedure
options.explanation: CONTRAST-ASSOCIATED ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (CA-AKI) is defined as a rise in serum creatinine >= 0.3 mg/dL or >= 50% within 48 to 72 hours following intravascular administration of iodinated contrast media. The primary pathophysiology involves contrast-induced renal medullary vasoconstriction, medullary hypoxia, and direct tubular epithelial cytotoxicity. Landmark clinical evidence from the large-scale PRESERVE (Prevention of Serious Adverse Events Following Angiography) randomized trial and KDIGO guidelines definitively established that: (1) INTRAVENOUS ISOTONIC VOLUME EXPANSION (with 0.9% normal saline or Lactated Ringer's, typically 1 to 1.5 mL/kg/h for 3 to 12 hours before and 6 to 12 hours after the procedure) IS THE ONLY INTERVENTION PROVEN TO REDUCE CA-AKI IN HIGH-RISK CKD PATIENTS; and (2) PHARMACOLOGICAL AGENTS PROVIDE ZERO BENEFIT: The PRESERVE trial definitively proved that ORAL N-ACETYLCYSTEINE (NAC) AND INTRAVENOUS SODIUM BICARBONATE ARE NO BETTER THAN ISOTONIC SALINE ALONE for preventing death, requirement for dialysis, or sustained decline in kidney function. Therefore, routine prescription of NAC or bicarbonate is no longer recommended. topic: Syncope Risk Stratification Inpatient Telemetry vs Outpatient Discharge
stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a sudden syncopal episode that occurred 2 hours ago. He was walking from his living room to the kitchen when he experienced a brief sensation of dizziness lasting less than 5 seconds, followed by complete loss of consciousness and collapse. His wife witnessed the event and states he was unconscious for approximately 30 seconds without tonic-clonic movements, tongue biting, or post-ictal confusion; he regained full orientation immediately upon awakening. He denies chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. Medical history includes an anterior wall myocardial infarction 3 years ago (stented LAD, baseline LVEF 38% on echocardiogram 6 months ago) and hypertension. Current medications include carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, and atorvastatin. Vital signs: blood pressure 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate 64/min, and oxygen saturation 98%. Orthostatic vital signs demonstrate no postural drop in blood pressure. Physical examination is unremarkable with no murmurs. 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus rhythm at 64/min with old Q waves in leads V1 through V3 and a QRS duration of 110 ms; there are no acute ST-T changes or high-degree AV block. Cardiac troponin I and electrolyte panel are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with an outpatient 48-hour Holter monitor and routine cardiology clinic follow-up in 4 weeks
options.explanation: Outpatient monitoring is reserved for low-risk vasovagal syncope with normal hearts; syncope with prior myocardial infarction and low EF carries high sudden death risk requiring inpatient telemetry.

options.text: Admission to an inpatient telemetry unit for continuous cardiac monitoring and evaluation for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)
options.explanation: This patient presents with SYNCOPE WITH HIGH-RISK FEATURES FOR CARDIAC ETIOLOGY. Clinical guidelines from the ACC/AHA/HRS and validated risk stratification scores (such as the Canadian Syncope Risk Score and San Francisco Syncope Rule) categorize syncope into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk: (1) HIGH-RISK FEATURES FOR CARDIOMYOPATHY / VENTRICULAR ARRHYTHMIA: (a) PRE-EXISTING STRUCTURAL HEART DISEASE (history of myocardial infarction, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction LVEF <= 35-40%); (b) Sudden-onset syncope without preceding prodrome (autonomic vasovagal symptoms like diaphoresis, warmth, or nausea); (c) Age >60-65 years; and (d) Abnormal baseline ECG (pathological Q waves indicating myocardial scar); (2) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: In patients with prior myocardial infarction and reduced LVEF, syncope is presumed to be caused by TRANSIENT VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA (VT) arising from reentry circuits at the border zone of the myocardial infarct scar until proven otherwise. This carries an annual sudden cardiac death risk >15-20%; and (3) MANAGEMENT: Mandatory INPATIENT TELEMETRY ADMISSION for continuous rhythm surveillance, repeat echocardiography, and evaluation for IMPLANTABLE CARDIOVERTER-DEFIBRILLATOR (ICD) PLACEMENT (or electrophysiological study). options.explanation: Vasovagal syncope requires classic situational or emotional triggers with prolonged prodromal nausea/warmth; sudden collapse in ischemic cardiomyopathy is never presumed vasovagal.

topic: Hospitalized Medical Patient Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis Padua Score
stem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the hospitalist service with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). She has spent the past 3 days resting in bed at home due to severe exertional dyspnea and is currently on bed rest with bathroom privileges. Medical history includes active stage II invasive ductal breast cancer (currently receiving oral letrozole hormonal therapy), hypertension, and obesity (BMI 33 kg/m2). Vital signs: blood pressure 138/82 mm Hg, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. Physical examination reveals bilateral expiratory wheezing, mild jugular venous distension, and 1+ bilateral pretibial edema without asymmetric calf tenderness or swelling. Laboratory tests show: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, platelet count 240,000/uL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73 m2), and normal coagulation parameters. She has no active bleeding or history of bleeding diathesis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan regarding venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis for this patient?

options.text: Mechanical thromboprophylaxis with pneumatic sequential compression devices (SCDs) alone without any anticoagulation
options.explanation: Mechanical compression monotherapy is indicated only when pharmacological anticoagulation is contraindicated due to active bleeding.

options.text: Administration of full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion
options.explanation: Full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation is indicated for confirmed acute thrombosis (PE or DVT), not for routine inpatient prophylaxis, and exposes her to unnecessary bleeding.

options.text: Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis with subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily (or unfractionated heparin 5,000 units three times daily)
options.explanation: HOSPITAL-ACQUIRED VENOUS THROMBOEMBOLISM (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism) is the leading cause of preventable hospital mortality. The American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) and American Society of Hematology (ASH) guidelines recommend using a validated risk-assessment model (such as the PADUA PREDICTION SCORE) to identify hospitalized medical patients who require pharmacological VTE prophylaxis: (1) PADUA SCORE CALCULATION: Active cancer (3 points), reduced mobility/bed rest >= 3 days (3 points), age >= 70 years (1 point), acute heart and/or respiratory failure (1 point), obesity BMI >= 30 (1 point). Total Padua score = 9 points (HIGH RISK OF VTE is defined as score >= 4, carrying an ~11% risk of symptomatic VTE without prophylaxis); (2) PHARMACOLOGICAL THROMBOPROPHYLAXIS: In high-risk medical inpatients without active bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia, PHARMACOLOGICAL PROPHYLAXIS IS STRONGLY RECOMMENDED. Preferred regimens include: SUBCUTANEOUS ENOXAPARIN 40 MG ONCE DAILY, or DALTEPARIN 5,000 units daily, or LOW-DOSE UNFRACTIONATED HEPARIN (LDUH) 5,000 UNITS SUBCUTANEOUSLY EVERY 8 HOURS. LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin due to lower rates of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and convenient once-daily dosing; and (3) MECHANICAL PROPHYLAXIS (graduated compression stockings or pneumatic compression devices) is reserved for patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation (active major bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia <50k).

options.text: Oral aspirin 81 mg daily as definitive pharmacological thromboprophylaxis for medical inpatients
options.explanation: Aspirin is inferior to LMWH/heparin and is not guideline-approved for VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized non-surgical medical patients.

options.text: Withholding all thromboprophylaxis because early ambulation with bathroom privileges provides sufficient protection
options.explanation: Bathroom privileges do not constitute full ambulation; medical patients with high Padua scores (>=4) remain at high risk of fatal PE without heparin prophylaxis.

topic: Nonvariceal Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding Post-Endoscopy PPI Regimen
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with hematemesis and melena for 12 hours. He takes daily over-the-counter naproxen for osteoarthritis. On arrival, he was hypotensive (BP 88/54 mm Hg) and tachycardic (HR 122/min); aggressive crystalloid resuscitation with 2 liters of Lactated Ringer's and transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells restored his blood pressure to 118/72 mm Hg. Emergency esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) performed 4 hours after admission reveals a 1.8-cm peptic ulcer in the posterior duodenal bulb with an ACTIVE PUMPING ARTERIAL SPURTER (Forrest class Ia). Successful dual endoscopic hemostasis is achieved using hemoclip application and thermal bipolar electrocoagulation, with complete cessation of bleeding. The patient is transferred to the step-down unit. Which of the following is the guideline-directed pharmacotherapy and duration recommended by the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) following successful endoscopic hemostasis of this high-risk ulcer?

options.text: Immediate transition to oral omeprazole 20 mg once daily with resumption of a regular diet today
options.explanation: Standard once-daily oral PPI therapy cannot maintain gastric pH >6.0 during the critical first 72 hours, resulting in early clot lysis and massive re-bleeding.

options.text: Intravenous ranitidine or famotidine 20 mg every 12 hours as preferred acid suppression
options.explanation: Histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) exhibit rapid tachyphylaxis within 24 hours, cannot sustain neutral gastric pH, and do not reduce ulcer re-bleeding.

options.text: Continuous intravenous octreotide infusion 50 mcg/hour for 5 days as first-line therapy
options.explanation: Octreotide is a somatostatin analog indicated for VARICEAL hemorrhage to reduce splanchnic blood flow; it has no proven role in arterial peptic ulcer bleeding.

options.text: High-dose intravenous proton pump inhibitor therapy (e.g., pantoprazole 80 mg bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion or 40 mg IV twice daily) for 72 hours
options.explanation: Peptic ulcer bleeding is the most common cause of nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Following successful endoscopic hemostasis of HIGH-RISK ULCER STIGMATA (Forrest Ia active spurting, Forrest Ib active oozing, or Forrest IIa non-bleeding visible vessel), guidelines from the ACG and International Consensus Group mandate: (1) HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS PROTON PUMP INHIBITOR (PPI) THERAPY FOR 72 HOURS: Intravenous pantoprazole or esomeprazole (either as an 80 mg IV bolus followed by continuous 8 mg/hour infusion, OR high-dose intermittent 40 to 80 mg IV twice daily) MUST BE CONTINUED FOR 72 CONSECUTIVE HOURS; (2) PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL MECHANISM: Blood clot formation and platelet aggregation are exquisitely pH-dependent; at gastric pH <6.0, pepsin lyses fibrin clots and platelets fail to aggregate, dissolving the hemostatic seal over the eroded duodenal artery. Sustained high-dose PPI therapy maintains intragastric pH >6.0, allowing permanent clot consolidation and reducing recurrent bleeding by >50%, surgical interventions, and mortality; (3) 72-HOUR TIMELINE: Upwards of 80% to 90% of ulcer re-bleeding occurs within the first 72 hours post-endoscopy; after 72 hours of stability, patients can be safely transitioned to oral PPI once daily; and (4) Testing for and eradicating Helicobacter pylori is mandatory.

options.explanation: The HALT-IT trial demonstrated that tranexamic acid does not reduce mortality in gastrointestinal bleeding and significantly increases venous thromboembolic complications.

topic: Septic Shock Fluid Resuscitation Balanced Crystalloids vs Normal Saline
stem: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with septic shock secondary to acute pyelonephritis. Vital signs on presentation: temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F), blood pressure 78/44 mm Hg (mean arterial pressure 55 mm Hg) despite 1 liter of fluid, heart rate 130/min, and respiratory rate 26/min. Laboratory evaluation reveals: WBC count 22,400/uL with 16% bands, serum sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L, serum creatinine elevated at 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), and arterial lactate 4.6 mmol/L. She is initiated on broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobial therapy and low-dose norepinephrine infusion. Ongoing aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation is planned to administer the remainder of the guideline-directed 30 mL/kg fluid bolus. Which of the following intravenous resuscitation fluids is recommended by the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines and the SMART trial as the preferred choice for this patient?

options.text: 0.9% Normal Saline (0.9% sodium chloride) infused at 500 mL/hour until blood pressure normalizes
options.explanation: Large-volume 0.9% normal saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction, increasing acute kidney injury and dialysis rates (SMART trial).

options.text: 6% Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) solution to rapidly restore intravascular oncotic pressure
options.explanation: Synthetic starches (HES) cause severe nephrotoxicity, accumulate in the reticuloendothelial system, and increase mortality and requirement for dialysis in sepsis.

options.text: 5% Dextrose in water (D5W) as rapid bolus fluid resuscitation
options.explanation: D5W is hypotonic and distributes throughout total body water (only ~8% remains intravascularly), causing cerebral edema without correcting intravascular hypovolemia.

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) transfusions to provide colloid volume expansion and clotting factors
options.explanation: FFP is indicated solely for active bleeding with severe coagulopathy; using plasma as a resuscitation volume expander causes transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI).

options.text: Balanced crystalloids (such as Lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte)
options.explanation: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) international guidelines issue a strong recommendation for INITIAL RESUSCITATION WITH AT LEAST 30 ML/KG OF INTRAVENOUS CRYSTALLOIDS within the first 3 hours of sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock. Crucially, the guidelines issue a definitive recommendation for BALANCED CRYSTALLOIDS (Lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte) OVER 0.9% NORMAL SALINE. The physiological and clinical superiority of balanced crystalloids was demonstrated in the landmark SMART (Isotonic Solutions and Major Adverse Renal Events Trial) and SALT-ED trials: (1) 0.9% NORMAL SALINE CONTAINS SUPRAPHYSIOLOGICAL CHLORIDE (154 mEq/L vs plasma chloride ~100 mEq/L). Infusing large volumes of normal saline causes HYPERCHLOREMIC METABOLIC ACIDOSIS; (2) High chloride delivery to the macula densa triggers tubuloglomerular feedback, leading to profound RENAL AFFERENT ARTERIOLAR VASOCONSTRICTION, reduced renal cortical perfusion, and reduced glomerular filtration rate; (3) In the SMART trial (>15,000 ICU patients), balanced crystalloids significantly reduced the composite endpoint of MAJOR ADVERSE KIDNEY EVENTS WITHIN 30 DAYS (MAKE30: death, new renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction) compared to saline; and (4) Hydroxyethyl starches are strictly contraindicated in sepsis due to increased mortality and renal replacement therapy.

subject: Medicine
topic: Diabetic Ketoacidosis Resolution Criteria and Subcutaneous Insulin Overlap
stem: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus was admitted to the intensive care unit 14 hours ago with severe diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) triggered by viral gastroenteritis. On admission, her venous blood glucose was 520 mg/dL, arterial pH was 7.12, serum bicarbonate was 8 mEq/L, serum beta-hydroxybutyrate was 6.8 mmol/L, and anion gap was 26 mEq/L. She has received aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline followed by 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline with potassium chloride, alongside continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. At this time, repeat laboratory evaluation reveals: venous blood glucose 162 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.36, serum sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.4 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (serum anion gap 16 mEq/L, calculated as [139 - (104 + 19)] = 16 mEq/L... wait, 139 - 123 = 16... let's ensure normal gap: serum chloride 106, bicarbonate 21 -> gap 139 - 127 = 12 mEq/L), and serum beta-hydroxybutyrate has decreased to 0.4 mmol/L (normal <0.5 mmol/L). She feels hungry and is alert, oriented, and tolerating oral fluids. The ICU resident prepares to stop the intravenous insulin infusion and order lunch. Which of the following is the most critical management step required prior to discontinuing the intravenous insulin infusion?

options.text: Administration of subcutaneous basal insulin (e.g., glargine) 2 to 4 hours prior to stopping the intravenous insulin infusion
options.explanation: DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS (DKA) is considered RESOLVED when ALL of the following criteria are met: (1) Blood glucose < 200 mg/dL; (2) Serum bicarbonate >= 18 mEq/L; (3) Venous pH > 7.30; (4) Normal serum anion gap (<= 12 mEq/L); and (5) The patient is alert and able to eat. This patient meets all criteria for DKA resolution. The MOST CRITICAL THERAPEUTIC ERROR IN DKA MANAGEMENT is the abrupt cessation of intravenous insulin without adequate subcutaneous basal insulin coverage. Intravenous regular insulin has an extremely short elimination half-life of ONLY 4 TO 5 MINUTES; once the infusion is turned off, circulating insulin levels plummet to zero within minutes. In contrast, subcutaneous basal insulin (such as insulin glargine or degludec) requires 2 TO 4 HOURS TO BE ABSORBED AND ESTABLISH THERAPEUTIC SYSTEMIC CIRCULATING LEVELS. If the intravenous infusion is stopped prematurely or concurrently with subcutaneous injection, the patient experiences an absolute 'INSULIN-DEFICIENT WINDOW' of 2 to 4 hours, which inevitably triggers rapid relapse of lipolysis, ketogenesis, and REBOUND KETOACIDOSIS. Guidelines from the ADA and Endocrine Society mandate: SUBCUTANEOUS BASAL INSULIN MUST BE ADMINISTERED 2 TO 4 HOURS BEFORE DISCONTINUING THE INTRAVENOUS INSULIN INFUSION (preferably administered at mealtime).

options.text: Immediate discontinuation of intravenous insulin followed by subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin lispro only if postprandial glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL
options.explanation: Discontinuing the IV infusion without prior basal insulin creates an absolute insulin deficiency window, triggering immediate rebound DKA within hours.

options.explanation: Urine ketones measure acetoacetate, which remains positive for days after beta-hydroxybutyrate has cleared; waiting for negative urine ketones inappropriately prolongs ICU stay.

options.explanation: The patient has type 1 diabetes mellitus; metformin is not indicated for type 1 diabetes, and she is not intubated.

options.explanation: Stopping dextrose while continuing insulin causes rapid, life-threatening hypoglycemia; dextrose must be infused while insulin is running once glucose is <200.

topic: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State Fluid Resuscitation and Osmolality Reduction
stem: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department from a skilled nursing facility with profound lethargy and confusion that has progressed over the past 4 days. She has had poor oral intake and decreased urine output. Medical history includes hypertension and stroke with mild residual hemiparesis. Vital signs: blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 16/min (normal unlabored breathing without Kussmaul respirations), and temperature 37.8 C. Physical examination reveals an obtunded woman with dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and poor skin turgor; there is no fruity odor to her breath. Laboratory evaluation reveals: venous blood glucose 980 mg/dL, arterial blood gas showing pH 7.38 and bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, serum sodium 152 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, chloride 114 mEq/L, and BUN 68 mg/dL with creatinine 2.8 mg/dL. Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.8 mmol/L (mild elevation, reference <0.5 mmol/L). Effective serum osmolality is calculated at 348 mOsm/kg (reference 275-295 mOsm/kg). Urinalysis shows 4+ glucose and trace ketones. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management priority for this patient?

options.text: Immediate high-dose intravenous regular insulin bolus (0.3 units/kg) followed by rapid lowering of glucose by >150 mg/dL/hour
options.explanation: Rapid insulin boluses without prior hydration drive water into intracellular compartments, precipitating vascular collapse and cerebral edema.

options.text: Aggressive intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (0.9% normal saline) at 1,000 mL/hour, delaying insulin until initial hydration is underway

options.text: Initiation of continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) for emergency clearance of hyperosmolar solutes
options.explanation: Hemodialysis is contraindicated; osmotic disequilibrium syndrome can occur. Gradual fluid resuscitation is the definitive therapy.

options.text: Administration of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics and immediate discharge back to the nursing facility
options.explanation: HHS carries an in-hospital mortality rate of 10-20% and requires intensive inpatient ICU resuscitation and monitoring.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Ischemic Stroke Blood Pressure Thresholds for Thrombolysis
stem: A 63-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 75 minutes after the sudden onset of left-sided facial droop, left arm and leg flaccid weakness, and severe dysarthria. Her baseline functional status was independent. On arrival, she is alert. Neurological examination reveals left hemiplegia, left hemineglect, and left central facial palsy; National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score is 16. Emergency non-contrast head CT demonstrates no acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or established hypodensity; the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) is 10. Blood glucose is 134 mg/dL, and platelet count and coagulation parameters are normal. Vital signs: blood pressure 198/112 mm Hg in both arms, heart rate 88/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The patient meets all clinical criteria for intravenous thrombolytic therapy with alteplase or tenecteplase, but her blood pressure exceeds the protocol threshold. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding blood pressure control and thrombolytic administration according to the AHA/ASA guidelines?

options.text: Immediate infusion of intravenous alteplase without lowering blood pressure, as thrombolysis takes absolute precedence
options.explanation: Administering thrombolytic therapy with blood pressure >185/110 mm Hg causes catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage with high fatal outcome.

options.text: Aggressive blood pressure lowering with intravenous nitroprusside targeting a systolic blood pressure of 110 to 120 mm Hg
options.explanation: Excessive blood pressure reduction (<130-140 mm Hg) collapses collateral flow to the ischemic penumbra, expanding the infarct core and worsening neurological deficits.

options.text: Cautious blood pressure lowering with intravenous labetalol or nicardipine to <185/110 mm Hg before initiating intravenous thrombolytic therapy, maintaining BP <180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours
options.explanation: According to the American Heart Association / American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) acute ischemic stroke guidelines, BLOOD PRESSURE THRESHOLDS DEPEND CRITICALLY ON WHETHER THE PATIENT IS ELIGIBLE FOR REPERFUSION THERAPY: (1) ELIGIBLE FOR IV THROMBOLYSIS (alteplase or tenecteplase): Blood pressure MUST BE LOWERED TO < 185/110 MM HG PRIOR TO INITIATING THROMBOLYTIC INFUSION. Once thrombolysis is initiated, BLOOD PRESSURE MUST BE MAINTAINED STRICTLY < 180/105 MM HG FOR AT LEAST THE FIRST 24 CONSECUTIVE HOURS. Administering thrombolytics with blood pressure >= 185/110 mm Hg dramatically increases the risk of catastrophic FATAL SYMPTOMATIC INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGE (sICH); (2) ANTIHYPERTENSIVE AGENTS OF CHOICE: Short-acting, titratable intravenous agents: LABETALOL (10-20 mg IV push over 1-2 minutes, repeatable) or NICARDIPINE continuous infusion (5 mg/h, titrated by 2.5 mg/h every 5-15 min, max 15 mg/h); (3) IN PATIENTS NOT RECEIVING REPERFUSION THERAPY: 'Permissive hypertension' is permitted up to 220/120 mm Hg to maintain collateral cerebral perfusion in the ischemic penumbra; and (4) Precipitous drops in blood pressure (>15-20% drop) must be avoided to prevent expanding the ischemic infarct core.

options.text: Withholding all thrombolytic therapy permanently because presentation blood pressure exceeded 185/110 mm Hg
options.explanation: Thrombolysis is not contraindicated simply because presentation BP is high; guidelines explicitly direct lowering BP to <185/110 to proceed with thrombolysis.

options.text: Administration of oral nifedipine immediate-release capsules to achieve rapid sublingual blood pressure control
options.explanation: Immediate-release oral nifedipine causes uncontrolled, catastrophic arterial hypotension, stroke extension, and myocardial infarction and is banned by the FDA.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage Blood Pressure Lowering Targets
stem: A 61-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and progressive right hemiplegia that began 90 minutes ago. He has longstanding poorly controlled hypertension and takes no antithrombotic medications. On arrival, he is somnolent but responsive to voice. Vital signs: blood pressure 218/124 mm Hg, heart rate 78/min, respiratory rate 18/min. Neurological examination reveals right hemiplegia, right facial droop, and expressive aphasia. Emergency non-contrast head CT demonstrates an acute 28-mL parenchymal hematoma centered in the left putamen with mild surrounding vasogenic edema and 3 mm of midline shift; there is no intraventricular hemorrhage. Point-of-care coagulation parameters and platelet counts are normal. An intravenous nicardipine infusion is initiated. Which of the following represents the guideline-directed blood pressure target and management strategy for this patient according to the AHA/ASA guidelines and the INTERACT2 / ATACH-2 trials?

options.text: Permissive hypertension allowing systolic blood pressure up to 220 mm Hg to maintain cerebral perfusion
options.explanation: Permissive hypertension applies to ischemic stroke, not ICH; allowing SBP up to 220 mm Hg in ICH causes massive hematoma expansion, brain herniation, and death.

options.text: Aggressive reduction of systolic blood pressure to <110 mm Hg within the first 30 minutes of presentation
options.explanation: Overly aggressive BP reduction (<120 mm Hg) does not improve functional outcomes and causes acute kidney injury and renal hypoperfusion (ATACH-2 trial).

options.text: Administration of intravenous mannitol 20% bolus as monotherapy for blood pressure control
options.explanation: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used for elevated intracranial pressure or impending herniation, not an antihypertensive agent.

options.text: Rapid, smooth lowering of systolic blood pressure to a target range of 130 to 150 mm Hg, avoiding acute hypotension <120 mm Hg
options.explanation: Acute spontaneous INTRACEREBRAL HEMORRHAGE (ICH) is a neurological emergency where elevated blood pressure drives HEMATOMA EXPANSION (which occurs in up to 35-40% of patients within the first 6 hours and is the leading cause of early neurological deterioration and death). Clinical practice guidelines from the AHA/ASA, informed by the INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 randomized clinical trials, establish: (1) SYSTOLIC BLOOD PRESSURE TARGET: For patients presenting with spontaneous ICH and systolic blood pressure between 150 and 220 mm Hg without contraindications, ACUTE LOWERING OF SBP TO A TARGET OF 130 TO 150 MM HG IS SAFE AND EFFECTIVE to prevent ongoing hematoma expansion and improve functional recovery; (2) AVOID AGGRESSIVE HYPOTENSION: ATACH-2 demonstrated that aggressively lowering SBP to <120 mm Hg (or dropping SBP by >60 mm Hg within an hour) provides NO additional functional benefit while significantly increasing the incidence of ACUTE RENAL ADVERSE EVENTS and renal hypoperfusion; and (3) PHARMACOTHERAPY OF CHOICE: Continuous titratable intravenous infusions such as NICARDIPINE (5-15 mg/h) or CLEVIDIPINE, or intermittent boluses of LABETALOL (10-20 mg IV), because they allow smooth, predictable blood pressure titration without triggering erratic rebound surges or precipitous hypotension.

options.text: Immediate referral for emergent craniotomy for evacuation of the deep basal ganglia hematoma
options.explanation: Routine operative evacuation of deep basal ganglia hematomas does not improve mortality or functional outcome compared to medical management (STICH trials).

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Hyperkalemia Membrane Stabilization and Cellular Shift Protocols
stem: A 62-year-old man with end-stage renal disease who missed his last two hemodialysis sessions is brought to the emergency department with severe generalized weakness, lethargy, and paresthesias in both feet. Vital signs: blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg, heart rate 42/min (regular bradycardia), and respiratory rate 18/min. Physical examination reveals an alert but weak man with diminished deep tendon reflexes and bilateral flaccid lower extremity weakness. Emergency 12-lead ECG demonstrates tall, peaked, narrow T waves with a shortened QT interval, widening of the QRS complex to 142 ms, flattening of P waves, and a prolonged PR interval (early sine wave morphology). Point-of-care venous blood gas reveals: serum potassium 7.8 mEq/L (severely elevated, reference 3.5-5.0 mEq/L), pH 7.24, and bicarbonate 14 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most critical immediate pharmacological intervention for this patient?

options.text: Immediate administration of regular insulin 10 units intravenously combined with 50% dextrose, deferring calcium
options.explanation: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly over 15-30 minutes but provides zero immediate membrane stabilization against fatal ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Administration of oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 grams as definitive acute therapy
options.explanation: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has a slow onset of 2-6 hours, carries risks of intestinal bowel necrosis, and is completely inadequate for acute emergency stabilization.

options.text: Immediate administration of high-dose oral patiromer 16.8 grams with a 1-liter normal saline flush
options.explanation: Gastrointestinal potassium binders require hours to bind luminal potassium and have no role in immediate acute resuscitation.

options.text: Performance of emergent transvenous pacemaker insertion prior to any medical therapy
options.explanation: Bradyarrhythmias in severe hyperkalemia are caused by hyperkalemic conduction block; infusing calcium immediately restores conduction velocity, obviating pacing.

options.text: Immediate intravenous administration of calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride) 10% solution over 2 to 3 minutes
options.explanation: This patient has LIFE-THREATENING SEVERE HYPERKALEMIA (serum potassium 7.8 mEq/L) complicated by ADVANCED ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC CONDUCTIVE CHANGES (peaked T waves, QRS widening, P wave loss, impending sine wave). The management of severe hyperkalemia follows a strict, sequential three-step hierarchy: (1) STEP 1: CARDIAC MEMBRANE STABILIZATION (MANDATORY IMMEDIATE FIRST STEP): INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM (10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate or calcium chloride infused over 2-3 minutes). Calcium does NOT lower serum potassium; rather, it increases the extracellular electrical threshold potential of cardiomyocytes, restoring the normal resting-to-threshold voltage gradient and reversing cardiotoxicity within 1 to 3 minutes. If ECG changes persist after 5 minutes, a second dose of calcium should be repeated; (2) STEP 2: CELLULAR POTASSIUM SHIFTING (transient reduction of serum potassium within 15-30 minutes): Regular insulin 10 units IV accompanied by 50 mL of 50% dextrose (D50W), combined with high-dose nebulized albuterol (10 to 20 mg); and (3) STEP 3: DEFINITIVE POTASSIUM ELIMINATION: Emergent hemodialysis (the definitive treatment in ESRD), loop diuretics (if residual urine output exists), or modern gastrointestinal cation exchangers (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate). Administering insulin or binders before calcium leaves the myocardium vulnerable to fatal ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Symptomatic Hyponatremia Hypertonic Saline and Correction Limits
stem: A 67-year-old man with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a witnessed 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home, followed by persistent obtundation. He has had poor oral intake, mild confusion, and anorexia over the past 5 days. On arrival, he is post-ictal and responds only to noxious stimuli. Vital signs: blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, heart rate 76/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and temperature 37.0 C. Physical examination reveals a euvolemic man: moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, no jugular venous distension, and absence of peripheral edema. Neurological examination reveals lethargy and diffuse hyperreflexia without focal cranial nerve palsies. Emergency laboratory testing reveals: serum sodium 112 mEq/L (severe hyponatremia), potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 78 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, serum osmolality 236 mOsm/kg (hypoosmolar), urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg (inappropriately concentrated), and urine sodium 68 mEq/L (elevated, >40 mEq/L). Thyroid and adrenal functions are normal. He is diagnosed with SYNDROME OF INAPPROPRIATE ANTIDIURESIS (SIAD / SIADH) secondary to paraneoplastic ectopic ADH secretion. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management plan regarding hypertonic saline administration and 24-hour sodium correction limits?

options.text: Administration of 3% hypertonic saline as a 100-mL intravenous bolus over 10 minutes (repeatable up to twice), aiming for a rapid 4 to 6 mEq/L rise in serum sodium to terminate neurological emergency, with a strict 24-hour correction ceiling of <= 8 mEq/L
options.explanation: This patient has SEVERE, SYMPTOMATIC, ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC HYPOOSMOLAR HYPONATREMIA (sodium 112 mEq/L) presenting with a LIFE-THREATENING NEUROLOGICAL EMERGENCY (generalized seizure, obtundation) due to paraneoplastic SIADH. In hyponatremia, brain swelling (cerebral edema) occurs because water moves down the osmotic gradient into hypertonic brain cells. In severe symptomatic hyponatremia, guidelines from the European Society of Endocrinology and American experts mandate: (1) IMMEDIATE 3% HYPERTONIC SALINE BOLUSES: Administer 100 ML OF 3% SODIUM CHLORIDE INTRAVENOUSLY OVER 10 MINUTES. This bolus can be repeated up to twice (total of three 100-mL boluses) at 10-to-20-minute intervals if severe neurological symptoms (seizures, coma) persist; (2) IMMEDIATE TARGET: A RAPID RISE OF ONLY 4 TO 6 MEQ/L IN SERUM SODIUM IS SUFFICIENT to alleviate brain swelling, reduce intracranial pressure, and terminate seizures; and (3) STRICT 24-HOUR CORRECTION LIMITS: Total sodium correction MUST NOT EXCEED 8 MEQ/L IN THE FIRST 24 CONSECUTIVE HOURS (and <= 6 mEq/L in high-risk patients with malnutrition, alcoholism, or liver disease). EXCEEDING THIS RATE RISKS OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (ODS / central pontine myelinolysis), a catastrophic, irreversible neurological condition causing spastic quadriplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, and 'locked-in' syndrome from oligodendrocyte dehydration.

options.text: Continuous infusion of 0.9% normal saline at 250 mL/hour until serum sodium reaches 130 mEq/L
options.explanation: In SIADH, infusing isotonic saline worsens hyponatremia ('desalination'): the infused sodium is excreted into hypertonic urine while free water is retained.

options.text: Administration of 3% hypertonic saline targeting complete normalization of serum sodium to 135 mEq/L within the first 12 hours
options.explanation: Correcting serum sodium by >8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours causes irreversible osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis).

options.text: Oral fluid restriction to 1,500 mL daily as sole therapy without hypertonic saline
options.explanation: Fluid restriction is the cornerstone of CHRONIC asymptomatic SIADH; in acute seizures or coma, it is far too slow and leaves cerebral edema untreated.

options.text: Immediate intravenous administration of tolvaptan 15 mg combined with a high-dose loop diuretic
options.explanation: Vasopressin receptor antagonists (vaptans) cause unpredictable, rapid aquatic diuresis with extreme rates of overcorrection and ODS, and are contraindicated in acute emergencies.

topic: Hypovolemic Hyponatremia Volume Resuscitation and Water Diuresis Surveillance
stem: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the hospitalist service after 4 days of intractable watery diarrhea, poor fluid intake, and vomiting secondary to viral gastroenteritis. She takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for hypertension. On arrival, she is weak and lethargic. Vital signs: blood pressure 94/56 mm Hg (lying) and 78/44 mm Hg (standing), heart rate 116/min (orthostatic tachycardia), and respiratory rate 16/min. Physical examination reveals dry, cracked oral mucous membranes, sunken orbits, and poor skin turgor with flat neck veins; there is no peripheral edema. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, chloride 84 mEq/L, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L, BUN 44 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL, indicating prerenal acute kidney injury). Serum osmolality is 250 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 540 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium is 12 mEq/L (<20 mEq/L, reflecting renal sodium avidity). Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan regarding fluid therapy and monitoring?

options.text: Oral fluid restriction to 800 mL daily as first-line therapy to promote negative water balance
options.explanation: Fluid restriction is indicated for euvolemic hyponatremia (SIADH); in hypovolemia, fluid restriction worsens shock, acute kidney injury, and ischemic collapse.

options.text: Intravenous infusion of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline) to restore effective circulating volume, with strict serial sodium monitoring every 2 to 4 hours to detect spontaneous rapid water diuresis
options.explanation: This patient has HYPOVOLEMIC HYPOOSMOLAR HYPONATREMIA, caused by gastrointestinal fluid loss compounded by thiazide diuretic use. Pathophysiology involves two distinct phases: (1) HYPOVOLEMIC PHASE: Profound arterial volume depletion triggers BARORECEPTOR-MEDIATED NON-OSMOTIC ADH SECRETION (vasopressin release overrides osmotic suppression to preserve intravascular volume). Concurrently, decreased renal perfusion stimulates proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption, producing concentrated urine with low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L); (2) TREATMENT OF HYPOVOLEMIA: Intravenous volume resuscitation with ISOTONIC (0.9%) NORMAL SALINE is the treatment of choice to restore effective circulating arterial blood volume; and (3) THE WATER DIURESIS PHENOMENON (CRITICAL SURVEILLANCE PEARL): As soon as normal saline restores intravascular volume, arterial baroreceptor stretch immediately SHUTS OFF NON-OSMOTIC ADH SECRETION. Without ADH, the collecting ducts become impermeable to water, triggering SUDDEN, PROFUSE SPONTANEOUS FREE WATER DIURESIS ('water dumping'). This abrupt water loss can cause serum sodium to escalate precipitously by >12 to 15 mEq/L in a few hours, placing the patient at catastrophic risk of OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME. Therefore, strict serial sodium monitoring every 2 to 4 hours is mandatory, and if rapid overcorrection begins, D5W or desmopressin (DDAVP) must be administered immediately to arrest sodium rise.

options.text: Administration of intravenous tolvaptan 30 mg to block V2 receptors and accelerate sodium correction
options.explanation: Tolvaptan causes massive free water excretion and is strictly contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia due to exacerbation of hypovolemic shock.

options.text: Intravenous infusion of 5% dextrose in water (D5W) at 150 mL/hour without any saline hydration
options.explanation: D5W contains no sodium and distributes throughout total body water, worsening hyponatremia and failing to restore effective circulating volume.

options.text: Continuation of hydrochlorothiazide to maintain blood pressure control while giving intravenous fluids
options.explanation: Thiazide diuretics directly inhibit NaCl reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and impair urinary diluting capacity; thiazides must be stopped immediately.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Hypernatremia Free Water Deficit and Safe Correction Limits
stem: An 82-year-old bedbound woman with advanced vascular dementia is brought to the emergency department from an adult foster home. The caregiver reports that the patient developed progressive dysphagia and fever over the past week and has had virtually no fluid intake for 4 days. On arrival, she is obtunded, responding only to deep sternal rub. Vital signs: blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, and temperature 37.9 C. Body weight is 50 kg (110 lb). Physical examination reveals dry, parched oral mucosa, sunken eyeballs, and doughy skin turgor. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum sodium 168 mEq/L (severe hypernatremia), potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 130 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, BUN 62 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.7 mg/dL). Serum osmolality is 352 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality is 780 mOsm/kg. Her calculated free water deficit is approximately 4.5 to 5.0 liters. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan regarding fluid replacement and the rate of sodium correction?

options.text: Rapid infusion of 5% dextrose in water (D5W) at 500 mL/hour targeting complete normalization of sodium to 140 mEq/L within 12 hours
options.explanation: Lowering serum sodium by >12 mEq/L in 24 hours causes acute osmotic water influx into brain cells, triggering catastrophic cerebral edema and fatal herniation.

options.text: Infusion of 3% hypertonic saline to equilibrate the osmolar gradient across the blood-brain barrier
options.explanation: Administering hypertonic saline in hypernatremia further escalates hyperosmolality, triggering pontine hemorrhage, circulatory overload, and death.

options.text: Gradual correction of hypernatremia using hypotonic fluids (such as 5% dextrose in water or 0.45% saline), strictly capping the rate of serum sodium reduction at <= 10 to 12 mEq/L per 24 hours (0.5 mEq/L/hour)
options.explanation: SEVERE HYPERNATREMIA (serum sodium >160 mEq/L) in an incapacitated older adult results from unreplaced free water deficit (inability to perceive or access water). When hypertonicity develops chronically (>48 hours), brain cells protect their cellular volume by generating INTRACELLULAR ORGANIC OSMOLYTES (idiogenic osmoles, including inositol, betaine, and taurine) to balance extracellular hypertonicity. In chronic hypernatremia, guideline principles mandate: (1) SAFE CORRECTION RATE: Serum sodium MUST BE LOWERED SLOWLY, AT A RATE NOT EXCEEDING 10 TO 12 MEQ/L IN 24 HOURS (approximately 0.5 mEq/L/hour), targeting a serum sodium of ~156-158 mEq/L at 24 hours; (2) CONSEQUENCES OF RAPID CORRECTION: Brain cells require 48 to 72 hours to clear idiogenic osmoles. If hypernatremia is corrected too rapidly using large volumes of hypotonic fluid, water rushes into brain cells along the osmotic gradient, precipitating SEVERE CEREBRAL EDEMA, SEIZURES, COMA, AND FATAL TENTORIAL HERNIATION; and (3) FLUID SELECTION: If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) is used initially to restore perfusion. Once hemodynamics are stable, FREE WATER DEFICIT IS REPLACED USING HYPOTONIC FLUIDS (D5W intravenously or water via nasogastric tube), calculated to replace the free water deficit plus ongoing insensible and urinary losses over 48 to 72 hours.

options.text: Rapid intravenous administration of furosemide 80 mg boluses to induce immediate natriuresis
options.explanation: Loop diuretics cause hypotonic fluid diuresis (water loss exceeding sodium loss), which directly worsens hypernatremia and volume depletion.

options.text: Withholding all intravenous fluids and administering oral desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.2 mg
options.explanation: Desmopressin is indicated for central diabetes insipidus; this patient has concentrated urine (780 mOsm/kg), proving normal intact endogenous ADH response.

topic: Acute Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure COPD Exacerbation Noninvasive Ventilation
stem: A 68-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (GOLD stage 3, baseline FEV1 42% predicted) is admitted to the hospitalist service with a 3-day history of worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, and productive cough with purulent green sputum. He has been using his home albuterol-ipratropium inhalers every 2 hours without relief. On arrival, he is in moderate respiratory distress, sitting upright and using accessory neck muscles to breathe. Vital signs: blood pressure 146/88 mm Hg, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/min improves his oxygen saturation to 91%. Physical examination reveals diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezing and distant heart sounds; there is no stridor or facial trauma. Arterial blood gas (ABG) on 2 L nasal cannula reveals: pH 7.28, PaCO2 64 mm Hg, PaO2 62 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis). He is alert, cooperative, and able to protect his airway and clear secretions. Nebulized bronchodilators and intravenous methylprednisolone are initiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in ventilatory management for this patient?

options.text: Immediate endotracheal intubation and initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation
options.explanation: Invasive mechanical ventilation carries high risks of ventilator-associated pneumonia, barotrauma, and weaning failure; NIPPV is the mandatory first-line trial in cooperative patients.

options.text: Increasing oxygen delivery via a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min targeting an oxygen saturation of 99% to 100%
options.explanation: Excessive hyperoxia in COPD exacerbations blunts hypoxic drive, worsens V/Q mismatch (Haldane effect), and triggers catastrophic hypercapnic coma (target SpO2 is 88-92%).

options.text: Administration of intravenous naloxone and flumazenil to stimulate spontaneous respiratory drive
options.explanation: The patient has COPD exacerbation with respiratory muscle fatigue, not opioid or benzodiazepine overdose; flumazenil precipitates refractory seizures in chronic users.

options.text: Initiation of non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV / BiPAP) with close monitoring of arterial blood gases
options.explanation: This patient has an ACUTE EXACERBATION OF CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE (AECOPD) complicated by ACUTE RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS (pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg). In acute hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to COPD exacerbation, guidelines from the American Thoracic Society (ATS) and European Respiratory Society (ERS) establish: (1) NON-INVASIVE POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (NIPPV / BiPAP) IS THE FIRST-LINE VENTILATORY INTERVENTION OF CHOICE. Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) provides: (a) Inspiratory positive airway pressure (IPAP) to augment tidal volume, offload fatigued respiratory muscles, and wash out carbon dioxide (reducing PaCO2); and (b) Expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) to counteract intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP), preventing dynamic airway collapse and improving alveolar recruitment and oxygenation; (2) PROVEN CLINICAL OUTCOMES: Extensive randomized controlled trial evidence demonstrates that NIPPV REDUCES THE NEED FOR INVASIVE ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION BY >60%, REDUCES IN-HOSPITAL MORTALITY BY >50%, and significantly shortens ICU and hospital length of stay compared to standard medical therapy alone; and (3) CRITERIA AND CONTRAINDICATIONS: NIPPV is indicated for acute respiratory acidosis (pH <= 7.35 and PaCO2 >= 45 mm Hg) in cooperative patients able to protect their airway. Absolute contraindications to NIPPV include: respiratory arrest, severe hemodynamic instability/shock, inability to protect the airway (coma, severe encephalopathy), facial trauma/burns, and excessive vomiting/bowel obstruction.

options.text: Placement of a high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) at 60 L/min as the proven superior ventilatory mode over BiPAP
options.explanation: While HFNC can provide oxygenation, BiPAP is the established gold standard with proven mortality reduction in hypercapnic COPD acidosis (pH <7.35).

topic: Massive Pulmonary Embolism Systemic Thrombolysis Indications
stem: A 54-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit 10 days following an uncomplicated total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Approximately 45 minutes ago, while walking to the bathroom, she experienced sudden severe dyspnea, diaphoresis, and collapse. On arrival in the ICU, she is pale, tachypneic, and diaphoretic. Vital signs: blood pressure 76/44 mm Hg (sustained hypotension despite 2 liters of Lactated Ringer's), heart rate 134/min (sinus tachycardia), respiratory rate 32/min, and oxygen saturation 86% on a non-rebreather mask. Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous distension of 12 cm H2O, an accentuated pulmonic component of S2, and a right ventricular third heart sound (S3 gallop); lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3 pattern and new right bundle branch block. Bedside point-of-care echocardiogram demonstrates marked right ventricular dilatation, severe hypokinesis of the RV free wall with sparing of the apex (McConnell sign), and a leftward bowing of the interventricular septum, with an underfilled, hyperdynamic left ventricle. Contrast chest CT angiogram demonstrates extensive bilateral saddle pulmonary emboli occluding the main pulmonary arterial bifurcations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management according to the AHA and ACCP guidelines?

options.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation with subcutaneous enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily as sole therapy, avoiding thrombolysis
options.explanation: Anticoagulation prevents new clot propagation but does not dissolve existing occlusive thrombus; in massive PE with cardiogenic shock, mortality exceeds 50% without thrombolysis.

options.text: Immediate placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter as definitive hemodynamic management
options.explanation: IVC filters do not dissolve the existing saddle embolus or relieve acute obstructive shock; filters are indicated only when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated.

options.text: Administration of high-dose intravenous furosemide 80 mg bolus to relieve right ventricular strain
options.explanation: Loop diuretics further reduce right ventricular preload, causing catastrophic total circulatory collapse in right ventricular failure.

options.text: Immediate transbronchial needle aspiration and balloon dilatation of the main pulmonary arteries
options.explanation: Bronchoscopy evaluates the tracheobronchial tree, not the intravascular pulmonary arterial bed, and carries no therapeutic role in pulmonary embolism.

options.text: Immediate administration of systemic intravenous thrombolytic therapy (e.g., alteplase 100 mg infused over 2 hours) or emergent catheter-directed embolectomy
options.explanation: PULMONARY EMBOLISM (PE) is risk-stratified into three distinct prognostic categories that dictate emergency therapy: (1) MASSIVE (HIGH-RISK) PULMONARY EMBOLISM: Defined as acute PE accompanied by SUSTAINED SYSTEMIC HYPOTENSION (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg for >15 minutes, or requiring vasopressors/inotropes, or cardiac arrest) NOT caused by hypovolemia, arrhythmia, or sepsis. Pathophysiology involves acute RV afterload mismatch leading to acute RV dilatation, RV ischemia, septal flattening, diminished LV filling, cardiogenic shock, and electrical pulseless arrest; (2) EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT: The American Heart Association (AHA) and CHEST guidelines establish a strong Class 1 recommendation: FOR PATIENTS WITH MASSIVE (HIGH-RISK) PE AND ACCEPTABLE BLEEDING RISK, SYSTEMIC INTRAVENOUS THROMBOLYTIC THERAPY (ALTEPLASE 100 MG INFUSED OVER 2 HOURS) IS THE IMMEDIATE LIFE-SAVING TREATMENT OF CHOICE. Thrombolysis rapidly dissolves the central occlusive pulmonary thrombus, reducing pulmonary vascular resistance, relieving RV strain, and restoring systemic cardiac output within 1 to 2 hours; (3) SURGICAL OR CATHETER EMBOLECTOMY: Is indicated for patients with massive PE who have absolute contraindications to thrombolysis (recent intracranial hemorrhage, active major bleeding) or who fail thrombolytic therapy; and (4) In contrast, SUBMASSIVE (intermediate-risk) PE is hemodynamically stable (SBP >= 90) but has RV strain or elevated troponin, and is managed with anticoagulation alone plus close ICU monitoring.

subject: Surgery
topic: Neutropenic Enterocolitis Conservative Medical Therapy vs Surgical Exploration
stem: A 38-year-old man undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia is admitted on post-chemotherapy day 12. He has been profoundly neutropenic for 8 days (absolute neutrophil count [ANC] 60/uL). Over the past 18 hours, he has developed high fevers, watery non-bloody diarrhea, and severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain with abdominal distension. Vital signs: temperature 39.1 C (102.4 F), blood pressure 114/72 mm Hg, heart rate 108/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. Physical examination reveals an acutely ill man; abdominal palpation reveals tenderness localized to the right lower quadrant and cecal area with mild voluntary guarding, but no involuntary muscular rigidity, rebound tenderness, or signs of generalized peritonitis. Bowel sounds are hypoactive. Complete blood count reveals WBC 400/uL, ANC 60/uL, and platelets 28,000/uL. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrates circumferential cecal and ascending colonic wall thickening of 8 mm (normal <3 mm) with mural edema, pericecal fat stranding, and a small amount of pericecal fluid; there is no pneumoperitoneum, free air, or localized abscess. Stool Clostridioides difficile toxin PCR is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Conservative medical management comprising bowel rest, intravenous fluid resuscitation, nasogastric decompression, and broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobial therapy covering Pseudomonas and anaerobes (e.g., cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam plus metronidazole)
options.explanation: This patient presents with NEUTROPENIC ENTEROCOLITIS (TYPHLITIS), a life-threatening necrotizing colitis classically involving the cecum and ascending colon in patients with profound, prolonged neutropenia (ANC < 500/uL). Pathogenesis involves chemotherapy-induced mucosal ulceration, combined with neutropenic impairment of host defenses, leading to secondary polymicrobial bacterial and fungal invasion of the bowel wall by bowel flora (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacterales, anaerobes like Bacteroides, and Clostridium species). In patients with typhlitis WHO DO NOT HAVE PERITONITIS, BOWEL PERFORATION, OR UNCONTROLLED HEMORRHAGE, the standard of care is CONSERVATIVE MEDICAL MANAGEMENT: (1) Complete bowel rest (NPO) and aggressive isotonic crystalloid hydration; (2) Nasogastric tube decompression if distension or ileus is present; (3) BROAD-SPECTRUM EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL COVERAGE: Monotherapy with piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem, OR cefepime combined with metronidazole (covering Pseudomonas, enteric Gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes); and (4) SURGICAL RESECTION (right hemicolectomy) IS STRONGLY DEFERRED in severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia due to catastrophic operative mortality (>50%). Surgical exploration is indicated ONLY for: (a) Free pneumoperitoneum (bowel perforation); (b) Refractory gastrointestinal hemorrhage; or (c) Progressive clinical deterioration and shock despite maximal medical therapy.

options.text: Immediate emergency exploratory laparotomy and right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis
